Adolf Hitler. The Austrian-born dictator of Nazi Germany from nineteen thirty-four to nineteen forty-five, Hitler was the architect of one of history's worst genocides. Rising from obscurity through nationalist politics during the economic chaos of the Weimar Republic, he consolidated totalitarian power, rearmed Germany, and invaded neighboring countries, triggering World War II.

Hitler's path to power began with his service as a soldier in the First World War. Afterward, he promoted the stab-in-the-back myth, blaming internal enemies for Germany's defeat. In nineteen twenty-five, he published Mein Kampf, a rambling autobiography outlining his extreme nationalist ideology and antisemitic conspiracy theories. His rise came partly through legal means—his Nazi Party won electoral support during the Great Depression, and he was appointed Chancellor in January nineteen thirty-three.

Once in power, he consolidated totalitarian control by eliminating internal party rivals during the Night of the Long Knives in nineteen thirty-four. He openly defied the Treaty of Versailles by rearming, remilitarizing the Rhineland, and annexing Austria and Czechoslovakia without military consequence. Then in nineteen forty-one, he ordered Operation Barbarossa, his massive invasion of the Soviet Union, which he viewed as a racial war for Lebensraum—living space.

His genocidal ideology and catastrophic leadership directly caused the deaths of tens of millions and the Holocaust. In nineteen forty-five, as Soviet and Western armies converged, he committed suicide in his Berlin bunker, leaving behind a catastrophic legacy.
